feedback: If a learner says the moths 'turned dark', point to the 'follow one moth' tag: that individual kept its colour the whole time — what changed is which moths survived to breed.
When the environment is toggled clean again and the ratio reverses, ask the learner to explain the reversal using survival of existing variants, not moths 'repainting' themselves.
If the learner expects an instant flip, slow the model down one generation at a time so they see the shift build up as more survivors of one colour reproduce.
Prompt: 'Where did the dark moths come from before the trees got sooty?' to surface that variation existed before the environment changed.
activities.intendedInsight: Adaptation is selection acting on pre-existing variation across generations: better-camouflaged individuals survive and leave more offspring, so the population's trait frequency shifts. An adult moth's inherited wing colour stays the same for its whole adult life.
learnerActions: Start with a pale-lichen tree and a moth population that is mostly light with a few dark moths (variation that already exists).

Each round, let a bird eat the moths it can most easily SEE; on the pale tree the dark moths stand out and are eaten, the survivors breed, and read the colour ratio off a live population graph as the next generation appears.
Slide the environment into the Industrial Revolution so soot blackens the bark; now the LIGHT moths are the visible ones. Run several more generations and watch the graph flip toward mostly dark.
Slide the air clean again and run more generations to watch the ratio reverse back toward pale.
Use a 'follow one moth' tag on a single individual across the rounds and confirm it NEVER changes colour — only which moths survive to breed changes.
State in your own words what changed: the population's mix of colours, not any single moth's colour.
activities.title: Run the generational selection model: watch the population shift, not the individual

feedback: A correct explanation says: variation already existed; the better-camouflaged variant survived and reproduced more, so over many generations the population's common colour/shape changed; no individual transformed itself.

If a learner explains the stick insect as 'growing twiggy on purpose' or because it 'needed to', remove intention: by chance some were already more twig-like, and those survived more — nothing wanted or planned anything.

If the learner keeps the explanation only at the peppered-moth example, ask them to re-run the structure (variation → differential survival → inheritance over generations) on the spider to check for transfer.
activities.intendedInsight: The same mechanism — differential survival of pre-existing variation, inherited across generations — explains the reversal and generalises to many camouflage and mimicry adaptations; it is not a one-off story about moths.
learnerActions: Explain, in writing or aloud, why pale moths became common again after air pollution fell (for example through clean-air laws) and trees got cleaner — using survival of existing variants, not moths changing themselves.
Answer: 'Could ONE adult moth, in its own life, change its wing colour from pale to dark to hide better? So what actually changed — the moth, or the population?'
Apply the same reasoning to a stick insect: did one stick insect grow twiggy on purpose, or did twig-like ones survive better over generations? Explain using differential survival and inheritance.
Apply it again to ant-mimicking spiders: explain how looking like an ant could help an individual survive and pass on that appearance.
activities.title: Explain the reversal and transfer to other animals (stick insects and ant-mimicking spiders)

feedback: If the learner uses intentional language ('they knew they had to blend in'), point out that variation already existed by chance and the environment only affected which variant survived more — no moth wanted or planned anything.
If the learner compresses the change into one season or one moth, ask them to tally colour across several generations so inheritance over time becomes explicit.
activities.intendedInsight: Natural selection is a filter acting on variation, not a conscious choice or a need-driven transformation, and it unfolds over many generations rather than within one lifetime.
learnerActions: Discuss the question 'Did the moth decide to change colour?' and defend your answer.
Respond to follow-ups that probe intention and timescale, e.g. 'Did the moths change because they needed to?' and 'Did this happen to one group of moths in a single summer?'
Restate the mechanism without using words like 'turned', 'changed to fit', or 'adapted itself'.
activities.title: Socratic discussion to surface and correct the Lamarckian idea

feedback: For the contrast question, the correct answer is that dark moths survived better; reject the 'turned dark' option and ask the learner to explain why in terms of survival and breeding.
If a match is made without a survival reason, ask 'how does this adaptation help the insect survive and leave offspring?'
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the distinction between individual change and population shift, and connect adaptations to the survival function they serve.
learnerActions: Order the peppered-moth events into the correct selection story (clean trees with mostly pale moths → soot darkens bark → dark moths better hidden → dark survivors breed more → population becomes mostly dark → clean air returns → pale moths favoured again).
Answer a contrasting question: 'Did the moth turn dark, or did dark moths survive better?' and justify the choice.

Match each animal to the function of its adaptation (stick insect's twig shape → hide from predators; ant-mimicking spider's ant-like look → fool predators; peppered moth's dark colouring on sooty bark → camouflage). Note that the spider is an arachnid, not an insect.
activities.title: Check understanding: sequence, contrast, and match
